description: Native vs cross-platform, and the constraints every phone app lives with.

screens.body:
Every mobile app is built one of two ways. Native means using the platform's own language and tools: Swift and SwiftUI for iPhone, Kotlin and Jetpack Compose for Android.

Cross-platform means writing one codebase that runs on both phones: React Native, Flutter, or .NET MAUI. The choice shapes your team, your budget, and how at home the app feels on each phone.

options: The platform's own language and tools
check.question: A native app is built with…

screens.heading: Two ways to build an app
screens.keyPoint: Native = per platform. Cross-platform = one codebase for both.

screens.body:
Native apps talk to the phone directly, with no middleman. That buys full access to every sensor and API, the best possible performance, and new OS features on day one.

The price: you build and maintain the app twice. Two codebases, two sets of bugs, two releases to push through two stores.

options: It runs on both phones from one codebase
You maintain one codebase per platform
check.question: The main cost of going native is…

screens.heading: Native: the direct route
screens.keyPoint: Best performance and access; double the maintenance.

screens.body:
React Native lets you write mobile apps in JavaScript or TypeScript. Flutter uses Dart and draws every pixel itself with its own rendering engine. One team ships to both stores, and fixes land everywhere at once.

The trade-off: you sit one layer away from the hardware. Brand-new platform features can arrive late, and weird platform-specific bugs are harder to chase through the framework.
screens.heading: Cross-platform: write once
screens.keyPoint: One team, both stores — with a framework in the middle.

screens.body:
A Progressive Web App is a website that installs onto the home screen and can work offline. No app store, no review queue, one link to share.

The catch: a PWA can't reach everything a native app can. Hardware features like Bluetooth, NFC, and background processing are limited or missing, especially on iOS. Great for content apps; risky for hardware-heavy ones.

options: No app store needed — it installs from the web
check.question: A PWA's biggest advantage is…

screens.heading: PWAs: the third door
screens.keyPoint: No store needed, but hardware access is limited.

screens.body:
Phones run on batteries, and your app shares that battery with everything else on the phone. Tight loops, constant location polling, and chatty network calls drain it and heat the phone — users notice, and they uninstall.

Batch your network requests instead of trickling them. Prefer push notifications over polling. Pause expensive work the moment the app goes to the background.

options: Polling the server every few seconds
Keeping GPS on in the background
check.question: To protect the battery, prefer…

screens.heading: Constraint: the battery
screens.keyPoint: Batch work, push instead of poll, rest in the background.

screens.body:
Phones have far less memory than laptops, and the OS will kill backgrounded apps without asking to free RAM. Design for interruption: a call, a text, a dead battery.

Save state early and often so the user returns exactly where they left off. Keep your memory footprint small — oversized image caches are a classic app killer.

options: Return exactly where they left off
check.question: When the OS kills your backgrounded app, the user should…

screens.heading: Constraint: memory and interruptions
screens.keyPoint: The OS can kill you anytime — save state constantly.

screens.body:
Mobile networks are slow, flaky, and sometimes gone entirely: tunnels, elevators, rural roads. Never assume a connection exists.

Cache what you can, queue what the user does while offline, and sync when the network returns. And always show honest loading states instead of a frozen, silent screen.

options: The app stays useful with no connection
The app needs wifi just to open
All data lives only on the server
check.question: Offline-first design means…

screens.heading: Constraint: the network
screens.keyPoint: Never assume a connection — cache, queue, sync.
